newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tycoon on trial over real estate scandal.
newsitem.headline: German tycoon on trial over real estate scandal.

text.p: A German real estate tycoon accused of causing one of the country's largest corporate scandals went on trial on Monday and a bankruptcy court judge said banks lost 2.2 billion marks ($1.3 billion) in the debacle.

Juergen Schneider, a former bricklayer who built one of the country's largest real estate empires, was expected to make a personal statement to a Frankfurt court at the outset of his trial on a series of fraud charges.

More than 100 journalists turned out for the trial's first day, the latest episode in a drama that has gripped Germany's attention and even inspired a feature film since Schneider has blamed Frankfurt's banks for the collapse of his group.
Schneider's wife, Claudia, is also accused of abetting a bankruptcy offence and will stand trial at a later date.
The banks deny any wrongdoing -- a view backed up by local prosecutors who pressed charges against Schneider after he was captured in Miami in 1995 following an international manhunt.

As the trial opened, a bankruptcy court judge in Cologne on Monday put a final estimate of bank losses in the scandal at 2.2 billion marks, while craftsmen who had done work for Schneider lost a total of 250 million marks.
"This is the amount banks are going to be stuck with," Judge Axel Rohrbeck told the Colonge newspaper Koelnischer Rundschau on Monday of the 2.2 billion marks.
Lawyers have not yet decided whether officials of major banks, embarrassed by the apparent ease with which they doled out their billions, should be called to the witness stand.

Prosecutors allege Schneider, who fled Germany shortly after his empire began to collapse in early 1994, fooled the banks into extending credit by overstating rental income from his properties and by forging bills.
Schneider, 63, faces charges of credit fraud, serious fraud and a bankruptcy offence but prosecutors say they will only try him initially on the fraud allegations.

If found guilty, he faces a maximum sentence of 15 years. But few experts expect Schneider, who has been held in custody since being extradited to Germany in February 1995, to receive a long prison sentence.
The tycoon gained fame by refurbishing historic hotels and stylish shopping malls in the post-unification property boom.
But his rental income was too low to repay his debts.

The collapse of Schneider's group, run from a massive villa on the outskirts of Frankfurt, sparked fears of a German real estate slump, left hundreds of small craftsmen fighting for their livelihoods and exposed his banks to public outrage.

Germany's biggest bank, Deutsche Bank AG, which bore the brunt of criticism for loose lending and lax supervision, accepted the resignations of four executives as a result of the debacle. The bank maintained the executives had not behaved dishonourably.

Deutsche, Schneider's largest creditor with an exposure of about 1.2 billion marks, made matters worse for itself when former Deutsche chief executive Hilmar Kopper dismissed as "peanuts" the millions of marks that Schneider owed to small tradesmen and builders. ($ = 1.739 German Marks)
